claims.text: The as-deposited FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy coating has relatively incoherent FCC/BCC phase interfaces.
Post-deposition heat treatment at 600°C for 2–4 hours in an inert atmosphere enhances FCC/BCC interface coherency.
Slow cooling after heat treatment minimizes thermal stresses.
Enhanced FCC/BCC interface coherency increases the coating's creep resistance.
Improved interface coherency increases the barrier to dislocation motion.
Improved interface coherency promotes dislocation pile-ups at FCC/BCC phase boundaries.
Dislocation pile-ups at reinforced phase boundaries distribute applied stress more effectively.
The proposed interface-mediated mechanism raises the stress threshold for creep deformation.
The tailored heat-treated coating will have a lower creep rate than an as-deposited or conventionally heat-treated coating.
The tailored heat-treated coating will have a higher stress threshold for creep initiation than the baseline coating.
The creep-resistance benefit persists under sustained stress while the FCC/BCC phases remain stable.
Temperatures above the phase-stability limit may diminish or reverse the creep-resistance benefit.
Insufficient control of the heat-treatment parameters may diminish or reverse the creep-resistance benefit.
Variability in the heat-treatment response could produce non-uniform changes in interface coherency.
Unanticipated diffusion or phase alterations could reduce the expected improvement in creep resistance.
